analysis.one_liner: Required federal regulators to refund overcharged electricity customers and cap Western wholesale power prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or House vote, dying in subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000-01 Western electricity crisis, wholesale power prices in California spiked far above what power actually cost to produce, and those costs showed up on household and business electric bills. This bill would have required the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the agency that oversees wholesale power sales, to order refunds, with interest, of any charges it found unjust or unreasonable. It would also have required FERC to set a maximum wholesale price for electricity sold in the Western region, based on the seller's actual cost plus a fair return, and to fine violators three times the amount involved.
analysis.who_benefits: California and other Western electricity customers. The bill would have clawed back wholesale overcharges and capped future wholesale prices at cost-based levels, which would have flowed through to household and business electric bills in a state where utilities were passing crisis-level wholesale costs to customers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires FERC to order refunds, with interest, of any portion of market-based electricity charges it finds unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential [S2][S3].

Requires FERC to establish a cost-based maximum price for wholesale electricity sold in the Western Systems Coordinating Council for periods after June 1, 2000, with mandatory refunds of prices paid above that maximum [S2][S3].
Lets any governor in the Western region petition FERC for a determination, which FERC must act on within 30 days, and imposes civil penalties of three times the amount involved for violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers — merchant generators and power marketers, many based outside California, that had been selling power at market-based rates far above production cost. They would have faced retroactive refunds with interest, a binding price cap going forward, and treble civil penalties.

drawbacks.text: Cost-based price caps set during a supply crunch can discourage investment in new generation and reduce incentives for out-of-state producers to ship power into the shortage region, the core good-faith objection to price controls in the electricity market [S3].

The refund authority would not reach charges paid more than two years before FERC's notice, and the bill's cap applied only to the Western region, limiting the relief and leaving pricing elsewhere untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Western consumers facing crisis-level bills, the upside — refunds and a cost-based cap on runaway wholesale prices — was substantial and direct. The main cost was the standard risk of price controls: if the cap was set too tightly, generators could withhold investment or power shipments, making shortages worse. The bill's own design acknowledged this by basing the cap on seller costs including a return on capital rather than an arbitrary number.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its energy subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner (D-CA) introduced the California Electricity Consumers Relief Act on January 30, 2001, with 13 other original cosponsors [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on January 30, 2001, and on February 14 was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 14 cosponsors — 13 House Democrats and 1 House Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wholesale electricity sellers that had collected crisis-level market-based prices were better off, because no refund order or Western price cap was ever mandated by Congress. California and Western ratepayers got no relief from this bill, which died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers who kept crisis prices

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor in January and March 2001.

for.name: 13 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including California members such as Susan Davis, Grace Napolitano, Mike Honda, Pete Stark, Robert Matsui, and Juanita Millender-McDonald.

for.name: 1 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Was the bill's sole Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it; it was sent to the energy subcommittee on February 14, 2001, and no action followed for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 14 cosponsors were 13 Democrats and 1 Republican, an overwhelmingly Democratic lineup; no vote was ever held, so the chamber's partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers
industries.note: The bill would have forced refunds of market-based rates found excessive and capped Western wholesale prices at seller cost plus a return, with treble penalties. Sellers' crisis-era profits were the direct target of the bill.

industries.industry: California electric utilities and their ratepayers
industries.note: Utilities buying wholesale power at crisis prices were passing those costs to customers; refunds and a cost-based cap would have cut both utilities' procurement costs and household bills.
